name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q01 - Value of delta n for ammonium chloride decomposition

questiontext.text:
We know that the relationship between \(K_c\) and \(K_p\) is

\[K_p = K_c (RT)^{\Delta n}\]

What would be the value of \(\Delta n\) for the reaction

\[\mathrm{NH_4Cl} (\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_3} (\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{HCl} (\mathrm{g})\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The balanced chemical equation is: \[\mathrm{NH_4Cl}(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_3}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{g})\] The relationship between the equilibrium constants is \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The quantity \(\Delta n\) represents the change in the number of moles of gaseous species during the reaction, calculated as the sum of stoichiometric coefficients of gaseous products minus the sum of stoichiometric coefficients of gaseous reactants. Solid and pure liquid phases do not contribute to \(\Delta n\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Delta n = \sum n_{\text{gaseous products}} - \sum n_{\text{gaseous reactants}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of moles of gaseous products: \[n_{\text{gaseous products}} = 1\text{ mol of NH}_3(\mathrm{g}) + 1\text{ mol of HCl}(\mathrm{g}) = 2\text{ mol}\] Number of moles of gaseous reactants: \[n_{\text{gaseous reactants}} = 0\text{ mol}\] because \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\) is in the solid state.
Subtracting the reactants from the products gives: \[\Delta n = 2 - 0 = 2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The stoichiometric values yield an integer net increase of two moles of gas. Therefore, the value of \(\Delta n\) for the reaction is \(2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q02 - Equilibrium constant when standard free energy is positive

questiontext.text: For the reaction \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\), the standard free energy is \(\Delta G^\circ > 0\). The equilibrium constant \((K)\) would be ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The chemical equilibrium is: \[\mathrm{H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\] The standard Gibbs free energy change of the reaction is strictly positive: \[\Delta G^\circ > 0\]

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The thermodynamic relationship connecting standard Gibbs free energy change and the equilibrium constant applies at absolute temperature \(T > 0\text{ K}\) with the universal gas constant \(R > 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The thermodynamic relationship is given by: \[\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K\] Rearranging for the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant: \[\ln K = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because \(\Delta G^\circ > 0\), \(R > 0\), and \(T > 0\), the fraction \(\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT}\) is strictly positive.
Consequently, the right-hand side is negative: \[\ln K < 0\] Taking the exponential on both sides: \[K = e^{\ln K} < e^0 \implies K < 1\] Since \(K\) is defined as a non-zero ratio of concentrations or partial pressures, it remains positive, hence \(0 < K < 1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A positive standard free energy change signifies a reactant-favoured equilibrium under standard state conditions, corresponding to an equilibrium constant less than 1. Therefore, the equilibrium constant satisfies \(K < 1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q03 - General characteristics of equilibria involving physical processes

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not a general characteristic of equilibria involving physical processes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Equilibrium involving physical processes is fundamentally dynamic in nature. At equilibrium, the rate of the forward physical transformation equals the rate of the reverse physical transformation, so microscopic changes continue unabated in both directions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Characteristics
Physical equilibria can be achieved and maintained only in a closed system at a given fixed temperature, preventing the exchange of matter with surroundings.
All measurable macroscopic properties of the system (such as vapor pressure, concentration, density, color, and temperature) remain strictly constant over time once equilibrium is established.
The opposing physical processes occur at identical rates, establishing a dynamic but stable steady state rather than a cessation of processes.

Step 3: Identification of Incorrect Statement
The claim that all the physical processes stop at equilibrium is incorrect because the state is dynamic rather than static.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the statement that is not a general characteristic of equilibria involving physical processes is that all the physical processes stop at equilibrium.

answer.text: Equilibrium is possible only in a closed system at a given temperature.
All measurable properties of the system remain constant.
All the physical processes stop at equilibrium.
The opposing processes occur at the same rate and there is dynamic but stable condition.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q04 - Equilibrium constant for phosphorus pentachloride decomposition reaction

questiontext.text: \(\text{PCl}_5\), \(\text{PCl}_3\) and \(\text{Cl}_2\) are at equilibrium at 500K in a closed container and their concentrations are \(0.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1}\), \(1.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1}\) and \(1.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1}\) respectively. The value of \(K_c\) for the reaction \(\text{PCl}_5 (\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3 (\text{g}) + \text{Cl}_2 (\text{g})\) will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Chemical equation: \[\text{PCl}_5(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(\text{g}) + \text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\] Equilibrium temperature: \(T = 500\text{ K}\)
Equilibrium concentrations:
\([\text{PCl}_5] = 0.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\)
\([\text{PCl}_3] = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\)
\([\text{Cl}_2] = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The equilibrium constant in terms of molar concentrations, \(K_c\), is formulated in accordance with the law of mass action using the equilibrium values of reactants and products.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[K_c = \frac{[\text{PCl}_3][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{PCl}_5]}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given numerical concentrations into the expression: \[K_c = \frac{(1.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol L}^{-1})(1.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol L}^{-1})}{0.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol L}^{-1}}\] Simplifying the arithmetic: \[K_c = \frac{1.44 \times 10^{-6}}{0.8 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{1.44}{0.8} \times 10^{-3} = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The numerator has order \(10^{-6}\) and denominator \(10^{-3}\), leading directly to \(1.8 \times 10^{-3}\). Therefore, the value of \(K_c\) for the reaction is \(1.8 \times 10^{-3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q05 - Incorrect statement regarding chemical and physical equilibria

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
In an isolated, perfectly insulated flask containing ice and water at equilibrium, the system undergoes no heat exchange or mass transfer, ensuring that the masses of ice and liquid water remain constant over time.
A catalyst accelerates the rates of forward and reverse reactions equally, leaving the equilibrium constant value unchanged.
For an exothermic reaction (\(\Delta H < 0\)), van 't Hoff's equation predicts that the equilibrium constant decreases as the temperature increases.

Step 2: Chemical Reaction of Iron Thiocyanate Equilibrium
The equilibrium between iron(III) nitrate and potassium thiocyanate forms blood-red \([\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}\): \[\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + \text{SCN}^-(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}(\text{aq})\] When oxalic acid (\(\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\)) is introduced, it dissociates into oxalate ions (\(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\)). Oxalate forms an exceptionally stable coordination complex with iron(III): \[\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 3\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}(\text{aq})\] This complexation consumes free \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) ions. According to Le Chatelier's principle, decreasing the concentration of \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) shifts the thiocyanate equilibrium in the reverse direction, decreasing the concentration of \([\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}\). As a result, the intensity of the red colour decreases, rather than increases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the incorrect statement is that the intensity of red colour increases when oxalic acid is added to a solution containing iron (III) nitrate and potassium thiocyanate.

answer.text: In equilibrium mixture of ice and water kept in perfectly insulated flask mass of ice and water does not change with time.
The intensity of red colour increases when oxalic acid is added to a solution containing iron (III) nitrate and potassium thiocyanate.
On addition of catalyst the equilibrium constant value is not affected.
Equilibrium constant for a reaction with negative \(\Delta H\) value decreases as the temperature increases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q06 - Enthalpy change prediction from temperature colour changes

questiontext.text:
When hydrochloric acid is added to cobalt nitrate solution at room temperature, the following reaction takes place and the reaction mixture becomes blue. On cooling the mixture it becomes pink. On the basis of this information mark the correct answer.

\[[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}(aq) + 4\text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}(aq) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\]

(pink)                (blue)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The equilibrium is: \[[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 4\text{Cl}^-(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}(\text{aq}) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})\] The hexaaqua complex is pink, and the tetrachlorido complex is blue.
The solution is blue at room temperature, and becomes pink when cooled.

Step 2: Relevant Principles
Le Chatelier's principle dictates that removing thermal energy (cooling) shifts an equilibrium in the direction of the reaction that produces heat (the exothermic process).
Conversely, supplying thermal energy (heating) shifts the equilibrium in the direction that absorbs heat (the endothermic process).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Evaluation
When cooled, the reaction mixture turns pink, indicating that the equilibrium shifts towards the pink reactant complex, \([\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}\).
Because cooling favours the reverse process, the reverse reaction must release heat and be exothermic (\(\Delta H_{\text{reverse}} < 0\)).
Consequently, the forward reaction must absorb heat, making it endothermic (\(\Delta H_{\text{forward}} > 0\)).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
An endothermic forward reaction has a positive standard enthalpy change. Therefore, \(\Delta H > 0\) for the reaction.

answer.text: The sign of \(\Delta H\) cannot be predicted on the basis of this information.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q07 - pH of pure water at elevated temperature

questiontext.text: The pH of neutral water at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) is 7.0. As the temperature increases, ionisation of water increases, however, the concentration of \(\text{H}^+\) ions and \(\text{OH}^-\) ions are equal. What will be the pH of pure water at \(60^\circ\text{C}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
At \(25^\circ\text{C}\), pure water is neutral with \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-] = 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) and \(\text{pH} = 7.0\).
At \(60^\circ\text{C}\), the self-ionisation of water increases while the neutrality condition \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]\) remains strictly preserved.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Formulae
The auto-ionisation of water is an endothermic process: \[\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{OH}^-(\text{aq}), \quad \Delta H > 0\] The ionic product of water is defined as: \[K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]\] For pure neutral water: \[[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_w}\] The pH is calculated from: \[\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Because ionisation absorbs heat, raising the temperature from \(25^\circ\text{C}\) to \(60^\circ\text{C}\) drives the equilibrium forward, causing \(K_w\) to increase above \(1.0 \times 10^{-14}\).
Consequently, the hydrogen ion concentration satisfies: \[[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_w} > 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\] Applying the negative logarithm: \[\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+] < -\log_{10}(1.0 \times 10^{-7}) = 7.0\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Although water remains strictly neutral because \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]\), the elevated concentration of \(\text{H}^+\) lowers the pH below 7.0. Therefore, the pH of pure water at \(60^\circ\text{C}\) is less than 7.0.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q08 - Order of pH for weak acid solutions

questiontext.text: The ionisation constant of an acid, \(K_a\), is the measure of strength of an acid. The \(K_a\) values of acetic acid, hypochlorous acid and formic acid are \(1.74 \times 10^{-5}\), \(3.0 \times 10^{-8}\) and \(1.8 \times 10^{-4}\) respectively. Which of the following orders of pH of 0.1 mol dm\(^{-3}\) solutions of these acids is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Acid concentration: \(C = 0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\) for each solution.
Given ionisation constants:
Acetic acid: \(K_a = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\)
Hypochlorous acid: \(K_a = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\)
Formic acid: \(K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a weak monobasic acid at concentration \(C\), the hydrogen ion concentration is: \[[\text{H}^+] \approx \sqrt{K_a C}\] The pH is given by: \[\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]\] A larger value of \(K_a\) indicates a greater extent of ionisation, resulting in a higher \([\text{H}^+]\) in solution. Because pH is inversely related to \([\text{H}^+]\), higher \([\text{H}^+]\) produces a lower pH value.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the ionisation constants: \[1.8 \times 10^{-4} > 1.74 \times 10^{-5} > 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\] The order of acid strength is: \[\text{Formic acid} > \text{Acetic acid} > \text{Hypochlorous acid}\] The order of hydrogen ion concentration is: \[[\text{H}^+]_{\text{formic}} > [\text{H}^+]_{\text{acetic}} > [\text{H}^+]_{\text{hypochlorous}}\] Applying the negative logarithm inverts the order for pH: \[\text{pH}_{\text{hypochlorous}} > \text{pH}_{\text{acetic}} > \text{pH}_{\text{formic}}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Hypochlorous acid is the weakest acid and dissociates least, resulting in the highest pH, whereas formic acid is the strongest and gives the lowest pH. Therefore, the correct order of pH is hypochlorous acid > acetic acid > formic acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q09 - Relationship between stepwise ionization constants of hydrogen sulfide

questiontext.text:
\(K_{a_1}\), \(K_{a_2}\) and \(K_{a_3}\) are the respective ionisation constants for the following reactions.

\[\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HS}^-\] \[\text{HS}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-}\] \[\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-}\]

The correct relationship between \(K_{a_1}\), \(K_{a_2}\) and \(K_{a_3}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The stepwise and overall equilibrium reactions with their equilibrium constants are: \[(1)\quad \text{H}_2\text{S} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HS}^-, \quad K_{a_1} = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{HS}^-]}{[\text{H}_2\text{S}]}\] \[(2)\quad \text{HS}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-}, \quad K_{a_2} = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{S}^{2-}]}{[\text{HS}^-]}\] \[(3)\quad \text{H}_2\text{S} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-}, \quad K_{a_3} = \frac{[\text{H}^+]^2[\text{S}^{2-}]}{[\text{H}_2\text{S}]}\]

Step 2: Relevant Principles
When an overall reaction is obtained by taking the sum of two individual chemical reactions, the equilibrium constant of the overall reaction equals the product of the equilibrium constants of the constituent reactions.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Adding reactions (1) and (2): \[\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{HS}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HS}^- + \text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-}\] Cancelling the intermediate species \(\text{HS}^-\) on both sides yields: \[\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-}\] which is identical to reaction (3).
Multiplying the expressions for \(K_{a_1}\) and \(K_{a_2}\): \[K_{a_1} \times K_{a_2} = \left(\frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{HS}^-]}{[\text{H}_2\text{S}]}\right)\left(\frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{S}^{2-}]}{[\text{HS}^-]}\right) = \frac{[\text{H}^+]^2[\text{S}^{2-}]}{[\text{H}_2\text{S}]} = K_{a_3}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The algebraic product of the stepwise equilibrium constants gives the overall constant. Therefore, the correct relationship is \(K_{a_3} = K_{a_1} \times K_{a_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q10 - Acidity of boron trifluoride explained by Lewis concept

questiontext.text: Acidity of \(\text{BF}_3\) can be explained on the basis of which of the following concepts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Acid-Base Definitions
Arrhenius theory defines acids as substances that dissociate in aqueous solution to yield \(\text{H}^+\) ions.
Bronsted-Lowry theory defines acids as chemical species capable of donating a proton (\(\text{H}^+\)).
Lewis theory defines acids as electron-pair acceptors.

Step 2: Electronic Structure and Behavior of Boron Trifluoride
In the boron trifluoride (\(\text{BF}_3\)) molecule, the central boron atom forms three single covalent bonds with fluorine atoms, accounting for six valence electrons.
Boron has an incomplete octet and possesses an empty unhybridised \(2p\) orbital.
Because \(\text{BF}_3\) contains no hydrogen atoms, it cannot produce \(\text{H}^+\) ions in water or donate protons to a base, meaning neither the Arrhenius nor the Bronsted-Lowry concept applies.
Owing to its electron deficiency and vacant orbital, \(\text{BF}_3\) readily accepts a lone pair of electrons from electron-rich donor species (such as ammonia) to form a coordinate bond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the acidity of \(\text{BF}_3\) is explained on the basis of the Lewis concept.

answer.text: Bronsted Lowry as well as Lewis concept.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q11 - Formation of buffer solution on mixing equal volumes

questiontext.text: Which of the following will produce a buffer solution when mixed in equal volumes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
A buffer solution resists changes in pH upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. A basic buffer consists of a weak base together with its conjugate acid (salt with a strong acid), while an acidic buffer consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base.

Step 2: Quantitative Analysis of the Mixtures
Let the volume of each solution mixed be \(V\text{ dm}^3\).
Mixing \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ NH}_4\text{OH}\) and \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ HCl}\) results in complete stoichiometric neutralisation: \[\text{NH}_4\text{OH} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\] Both reactants are fully consumed, producing only the salt \(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\), which gives an unbuffered acidic salt solution.
Mixing \(0.05\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ NH}_4\text{OH}\) and \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ HCl}\) leaves excess strong acid \(\text{HCl}\), producing a strongly acidic unbuffered solution.
Mixing \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ CH}_3\text{COONa}\) and \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ NaOH}\) contains a salt and a strong base without the weak conjugate acid \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\), so it cannot function as a buffer.
Mixing \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ NH}_4\text{OH}\) and \(0.05\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ HCl}\): \[\text{Initial moles of NH}_4\text{OH} = 0.1 \times V\] \[\text{Initial moles of HCl} = 0.05 \times V\] Reaction with strong acid consumes \(0.05 \times V\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\): \[\text{Moles of NH}_4\text{Cl formed} = 0.05 \times V\] \[\text{Moles of unreacted NH}_4\text{OH remaining} = (0.1 - 0.05) \times V = 0.05 \times V\] Because the resulting solution contains significant and equimolar concentrations of both a weak base (\(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\)) and its conjugate acid salt (\(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\), forming an effective basic buffer solution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, mixing equal volumes of \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ NH}_4\text{OH}\) and \(0.05\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ HCl}\) produces a buffer solution.

answer.text: 0.1 mol dm\(^{-3}\) \(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\) and 0.1 mol dm\(^{-3}\) HCl
0.05 mol dm\(^{-3}\) \(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\) and 0.1 mol dm\(^{-3}\) HCl
0.1 mol dm\(^{-3}\) \(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\) and 0.05 mol dm\(^{-3}\) HCl

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q12 - Highest solubility of silver chloride in aqueous ammonia

questiontext.text: In which of the following solvents is silver chloride most soluble?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
Silver chloride (\(\text{AgCl}\)) is a sparingly soluble salt governed by the dissolution equilibrium: \[\text{AgCl}(\text{s}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})\] Addition of common ions (\(\text{Ag}^+\) or \(\text{Cl}^-\)) decreases its solubility via the common ion effect.
Formation of a soluble coordination complex removes free silver ions from solution, driving the dissolution equilibrium forward.

Step 2: Comparison of Solvents
In \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ AgNO}_3\), the high concentration of \(\text{Ag}^+\) common ions suppresses the dissolution of \(\text{AgCl}\).
In \(0.1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\text{ HCl}\), the high concentration of \(\text{Cl}^-\) common ions suppresses the dissolution of \(\text{AgCl}\).
In pure water, dissolution is limited strictly by the solubility product constant \(K_{\text{sp}} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-10}\), giving a low solubility of \(\approx 1.34 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).
In aqueous ammonia (\(\text{NH}_3\)), ammonia molecules coordinate with silver ions to form the stable diammine silver complex: \[\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + 2\text{NH}_3(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+(\text{aq})\] The overall dissolution process is: \[\text{AgCl}(\text{s}) + 2\text{NH}_3(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})\] Due to the large formation constant of the complex (\(K_f \approx 1.7 \times 10^7\)), free \(\text{Ag}^+\) ions are continuously sequestered, shifting the equilibrium significantly forward and resulting in far greater solubility than in water or common-ion solutions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, silver chloride is most soluble in aqueous ammonia.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q13 - Calculation of pH of acetic acid solution

questiontext.text: What will be the value of pH of 0.01 mol dm\(^{-3}\) \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) (\(K_a = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concentration of acetic acid solution: \(C = 0.01\text{ mol dm}^{-3} = 10^{-2}\text{ M}\)
Acid dissociation constant: \(K_a = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Acetic acid is a weak monobasic acid that ionises according to \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}^+\). Since the degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a / C} \ll 1\), the undissociated acid concentration remains approximately equal to \(C\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a C}\] \[\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the \([\text{H}^+]\) formula: \[[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{(1.74 \times 10^{-5})(10^{-2})} = \sqrt{1.74 \times 10^{-7}} = \sqrt{17.4 \times 10^{-8}}\] Evaluating the square root: \[\sqrt{17.4} \approx 4.17\] \[[\text{H}^+] \approx 4.17 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\] Calculate the pH: \[\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(4.17 \times 10^{-4}) = 4 - \log_{10}(4.17)\] Using \(\log_{10}(4.17) \approx 0.620\): \[\text{pH} = 4 - 0.620 = 3.38 \approx 3.4\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The degree of dissociation is \(\alpha = \frac{4.17 \times 10^{-4}}{0.01} = 0.0417\), which is less than \(5\%\), validating the approximation. Therefore, the value of pH of the acetic acid solution is \(3.4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q14 - Value of pH of ammonium acetate solution

questiontext.text: \(K_a\) for \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) is \(1.8 \times 10^{-5}\) and \(K_b\) for \(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\) is \(1.8 \times 10^{-5}\). The pH of ammonium acetate will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Acid dissociation constant: \(K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\)
Base dissociation constant: \(K_b = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\)
Ammonium acetate (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COONH}_4\)) is a salt formed from a weak acid (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)) and a weak base (\(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both the cation and the anion undergo hydrolysis in aqueous solution. For salts of a weak acid and a weak base, the pH depends on the relative values of \(\text{p}K_a\) and \(\text{p}K_b\) and is independent of salt concentration at moderate dilutions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The pH of a solution of a salt of a weak acid and a weak base is given by: \[\text{pH} = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a - \text{p}K_b)\] where \(\text{p}K_a = -\log_{10}K_a\) and \(\text{p}K_b = -\log_{10}K_b\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since the numerical values are identical: \[K_a = K_b = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\] Their negative logarithms are also identical: \[\text{p}K_a = \text{p}K_b = -\log_{10}(1.8 \times 10^{-5}) \approx 4.74\] Substituting into the formula: \[\text{pH} = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(4.74 - 4.74) = 7 + 0 = 7.0\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because the acid and base have equal dissociation constants, the production of \(\text{H}^+\) by cation hydrolysis balances the production of \(\text{OH}^-\) by anion hydrolysis, yielding a neutral solution. Therefore, the pH of ammonium acetate will be \(7.0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q15 - Standard free energy change at half completion

questiontext.text: Which of the following options will be correct for the stage of half completion of the reaction \(A \rightleftharpoons B\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Chemical equilibrium: \(A \rightleftharpoons B\)
The system is at the stage of half completion, meaning half of the initial quantity of reactant \(A\) has converted into product \(B\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the initial concentration of \(A\) be \(c_0\) and that of \(B\) be 0.
At half completion, \([A] = c_0 - 0.5c_0 = 0.5c_0\) and \([B] = 0.5c_0\).
Thus, at equilibrium at this point, \([A] = [B]\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The equilibrium constant is given by: \[K = \frac{[B]}{[A]}\] The standard Gibbs free energy change of the reaction relates to the equilibrium constant by: \[\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the concentrations into the expression for \(K\): \[K = \frac{0.5c_0}{0.5c_0} = 1\] Substitute \(K = 1\) into the free energy equation: \[\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln(1)\] Because the natural logarithm of unity is zero: \[\Delta G^\circ = 0\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
When reactants and products are present in equal amounts at equilibrium, the equilibrium constant is 1 and the standard free energy change is 0. Therefore, \(\Delta G^\circ = 0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q16 - Effect of pressure change on equilibrium constant

questiontext.text:
On increasing the pressure, in which direction will the gas phase reaction proceed to re-establish equilibrium, is predicted by applying the Le Chatelier's principle. Consider the reaction.

\[\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})\]

Which of the following is correct, if the total pressure at which the equilibrium is established, is increased without changing the temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
The equilibrium constant \(K\) of a chemical reaction is defined by thermodynamics as: \[\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K \implies K = e^{-\Delta G^\circ / RT}\] For a given reaction, the standard Gibbs free energy change \(\Delta G^\circ\) depends only on temperature. Therefore, \(K\) is strictly a function of temperature and is completely independent of pressure.

Step 2: Effect of Pressure on Equilibrium Shift versus Equilibrium Constant
In the gas phase synthesis of ammonia: \[\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})\] the reaction proceeds with a decrease in the number of gaseous moles from 4 moles of reactants to 2 moles of product (\(\Delta n = -2\)).
According to Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the total pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift in the forward direction towards fewer moles of gas.
This shift alters the equilibrium concentrations and partial pressures in such a way that the reaction quotient \(Q\) remains equal to the equilibrium constant \(K\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Since the temperature is held constant, the value of the equilibrium constant remains unchanged. Therefore, \(K\) will remain same.

answer.text: \(K\) will increase initially and decrease when pressure is very high

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q17 - Order of vapour pressure based on boiling point

questiontext.text: What will be the correct order of vapour pressure of water, acetone and ether at \(30^\circ\text{C}\). Given that among these compounds, water has maximum boiling point and ether has minimum boiling point?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three volatile liquids: water, acetone, and ether at \(30^\circ\text{C}\).
Water has the maximum boiling point, and ether has the minimum boiling point.
The boiling point order is: \[\text{Water} > \text{Acetone} > \text{Ether}\]

Step 2: Relevant Principles
Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour in equilibrium with its liquid phase at a specified temperature.
A higher boiling point reflects stronger intermolecular forces of attraction, meaning molecules require more energy to escape into the gas phase, which produces a lower vapour pressure at any given temperature.
Conversely, weaker intermolecular attractive forces allow molecules to escape readily into the vapour phase, yielding a lower boiling point and a higher vapour pressure.
Thus, at any constant temperature, vapour pressure is inversely related to boiling point.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Water has strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, giving it the highest boiling point and consequently the lowest vapour pressure.
Ether possesses weak intermolecular forces, giving it the lowest boiling point and consequently the highest vapour pressure.
Acetone has intermediate dipole-dipole attractions, resulting in an intermediate boiling point and intermediate vapour pressure.
Inverting the boiling point order gives the vapour pressure order at \(30^\circ\text{C}\): \[\text{Water} < \text{Acetone} < \text{Ether}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The compound with the lowest boiling point exhibits the highest volatility and vapour pressure. Therefore, the correct order of vapour pressure is Water < acetone < ether.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q18 - Calculation of equilibrium constant for reverse reaction

questiontext.text:
At 500 K, equilibrium constant, \(K_c\), for the following reaction is 5.

\[\frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2(\text{g}) + \frac{1}{2}\text{I}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{HI}(\text{g})\]

What would be the equilibrium constant \(K_c\) for the reaction

\[2\text{HI}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(\text{g}) + \text{I}_2(\text{g})\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reference reaction: \[\frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2(\text{g}) + \frac{1}{2}\text{I}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{HI}(\text{g}), \quad K_{c_1} = 5\] Target reaction: \[2\text{HI}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(\text{g}) + \text{I}_2(\text{g}), \quad K_{c_2} = ?\] Temperature is constant at \(T = 500\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The equilibrium constants follow the law of mass action.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From the law of chemical equilibrium: \[K_{c_1} = \frac{[\text{HI}]}{[\text{H}_2]^{1/2}[\text{I}_2]^{1/2}} = 5\] \[K_{c_2} = \frac{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}{[\text{HI}]^2}\] When a reaction is reversed, its equilibrium constant is inverted: \(K' = 1/K\).
When stoichiometric coefficients are multiplied by a factor \(n\), the new equilibrium constant is raised to the power \(n\): \(K'' = (K')^n\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Reversing the reference reaction gives: \[\text{HI}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2(\text{g}) + \frac{1}{2}\text{I}_2(\text{g}), \quad K' = \frac{1}{K_{c_1}} = \frac{1}{5}\] Multiplying this reversed reaction by 2 produces the target reaction: \[2\text{HI}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(\text{g}) + \text{I}_2(\text{g})\] The corresponding equilibrium constant is: \[K_{c_2} = (K')^2 = \left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{25} = 0.04\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Calculating the decimal value gives \(1/25 = 0.04\). Therefore, the equilibrium constant \(K_c\) for the reaction is \(0.04\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q19 - Effect of argon addition at constant volume

questiontext.text: In which of the following reactions, the equilibrium remains unaffected on addition of small amount of argon at constant volume?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
Argon is a noble, chemically unreactive gas that does not participate in any chemical reactions with the reactants or products.
When an inert gas is added to a system kept at constant volume, the total pressure increases because the total number of moles of gas increases.
However, the molar concentration of any reacting gas \(i\) is given by: \[c_i = \frac{n_i}{V}\] where \(n_i\) is the moles of species \(i\) and \(V\) is the container volume.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reactions
Because the volume \(V\) is kept strictly constant and the number of moles \(n_i\) of each reacting gas does not change upon adding argon, the molar concentration of each reactant and product remains completely unaltered.
Likewise, the partial pressure of each gas, \(p_i = c_i RT\), remains unchanged at constant temperature.
Because the partial pressures and concentrations of all reacting components are unaltered, the reaction quotient \(Q\) remains identical to \(K\) for any reaction, regardless of whether \(\Delta n = 0\), \(\Delta n > 0\), or \(\Delta n < 0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Addition of an inert gas at constant volume has no effect on chemical equilibrium in any reaction. Therefore, the equilibrium will remain unaffected in all the three cases.

answer.text: The equilibrium will remain unaffected in all the three cases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q20 - Thermodynamic properties and direction of dinitrogen tetroxide reaction

questiontext.text: For the reaction \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(\text{g})\), the value of \(K\) is 50 at 400 K and 1700 at 500 K. Which of the following options is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Chemical reaction: \[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(\text{g})\] At \(T_1 = 400\text{ K}\), \(K_1 = 50\).
At \(T_2 = 500\text{ K}\), \(K_2 = 1700\).
Partial pressures mixed at \(400\text{ K}\): \(p_{\text{NO}_2} = 20\text{ bar}\), \(p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} = 2\text{ bar}\).

Step 2: Analysis of Enthalpy Change
According to van 't Hoff's equation: \[\ln\left(\frac{K_2}{K_1}\right) = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)\] As the temperature increases from \(400\text{ K}\) to \(500\text{ K}\), the value of \(K\) increases from 50 to 1700. Since an increase in temperature increases the equilibrium constant, the forward reaction absorbs heat, which means \(\Delta H^\circ > 0\) and the reaction is endothermic. Thus, the statement that the reaction is endothermic is correct, while the claim that it is exothermic is incorrect.

Step 3: Calculation of Reaction Quotient
At \(400\text{ K}\), the reaction quotient \(Q_p\) for the mixture is: \[Q_p = \frac{p_{\text{NO}_2}^2}{p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4}} = \frac{(20\text{ bar})^2}{2\text{ bar}} = \frac{400}{2} = 200\] Comparing \(Q_p\) with the equilibrium constant at \(400\text{ K}\) (\(K = 50\)): \[Q_p (200) > K (50)\] Because \(Q_p > K\), the system must proceed in the reverse direction to attain equilibrium, which means more \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(\text{g})\) will be formed. Thus, this statement is correct.

Step 4: Analysis of Entropy Change
In the reaction \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(\text{g})\), one mole of gas decomposes to produce two moles of gas: \[\Delta n_{\text{g}} = 2 - 1 = +1 > 0\] Because the number of gas molecules increases, the randomness and disorder of the system increase, meaning the entropy of the system increases (\(\Delta S^\circ > 0\)). Thus, this statement is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct conclusions are that the reaction is endothermic, more \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(\text{g})\) will be formed when mixed at the given partial pressures, and the entropy of the system increases.

answer.text: If \(\text{NO}_2(\text{g})\) and \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(\text{g})\) are mixed at 400 K at partial pressures 20 bar and 2 bar respectively, more \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(\text{g})\) will be formed.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MCQ_Q21 - Equilibrium temperature between solid and liquid phases

questiontext.text: At a particular temperature and atmospheric pressure, the solid and liquid phases of a pure substance can exist in equilibrium. Which of the following term defines this temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
For any pure substance at constant atmospheric pressure (1 atm or 1.013 bar), the solid and liquid phases can coexist in physical equilibrium: \[\text{Solid} \rightleftharpoons \text{Liquid}\] This state represents the transition temperature between the solid and liquid phases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Terms
When solid transitions to liquid at standard atmospheric pressure, this equilibrium temperature is termed the normal melting point.
When liquid transitions to solid at standard atmospheric pressure, this identical equilibrium temperature is termed the freezing point (or normal freezing point).
Boiling point refers to the temperature at which the liquid and vapour phases exist in equilibrium at 1 atm.
Equilibrium temperature is a generic term that describes any thermodynamic equilibrium rather than specifically defining the solid-liquid equilibrium under standard atmospheric pressure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the terms defining this temperature are the normal melting point and the freezing point.
